lesson.title: Fight or Flight in a Bottle: Adrenaline's Emergency Broadcast
lesson.summary: Adrenaline, also called epinephrine, is the hormone, and in some contexts neurotransmitter, that powers the body's fight or flight response, flooding the bloodstream within seconds to prepare the heart, lungs, and muscles for immediate action. It shows the hormonal system operating in its fastest, most dramatic mode.
lesson.body:
The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis introduced in the last chapter describes the body's slower, sustained response to stress, one that takes minutes to fully ramp up as cortisol circulates. Adrenaline, also called epinephrine, is that response's faster partner, capable of reaching the bloodstream and producing noticeable effects within just a few seconds of a perceived threat, long before cortisol levels have meaningfully risen.

Adrenaline is released mainly by the adrenal medulla, the inner core of the adrenal glands sitting atop the kidneys. What makes this release so fast is an unusual wiring arrangement: rather than being triggered by a slower hormonal signal traveling through the bloodstream, the adrenal medulla receives direct input from the sympathetic nervous system. When the hypothalamus perceives a threat, signals travel almost immediately down through the spinal cord along sympathetic nerve fibers straight to the adrenal medulla, triggering a near instantaneous surge of adrenaline into the bloodstream, a rare case of a gland being controlled directly by neural signaling rather than by another hormone.

Once in the bloodstream, adrenaline binds adrenergic receptors located on organs throughout the body, producing the coordinated set of changes commonly known as the fight or flight response. Heart rate and the force of each heartbeat increase, the airways in the lungs widen to allow in more oxygen, blood vessels supplying the skin and digestive organs constrict while vessels supplying the skeletal muscles widen, rerouting blood flow toward the tissues most likely to be needed for immediate physical action, the liver releases stored glucose into the bloodstream for quick energy, and the pupils dilate. All of this typically unfolds within seconds.

Adrenaline also illustrates the dual hormone and neurotransmitter role described in the previous chapter. Its close chemical relative, noradrenaline, or norepinephrine, is released by neurons of the sympathetic nervous system to act locally on nearby organs as a neurotransmitter, while adrenaline released by the adrenal medulla into the bloodstream acts more broadly as a hormone, reaching tissues throughout the entire body. Both belong to the same chemical family and act on closely related receptors, differing mainly in the scale and reach of their effects.

Consider a driver who has to swerve suddenly to avoid a collision. In the instant before any conscious, deliberate thought fully forms, an adrenaline surge has often already increased heart rate, sharpened alertness, and tensed the muscles, allowing for a faster physical reaction than calm reasoning alone could produce. Afterward, the lingering shakiness and racing heartbeat that can persist for several minutes once the danger has passed reflect a key difference from synaptic neurotransmission: adrenaline circulating through the bloodstream takes real time to be cleared away, unlike a synaptic signal that ends in a fraction of a second.
